topics.title: Shortest routes
topics.outcome: Find the fewest-edges route and unreachable vertices
topics.goal: Use BFS to find the route with the fewest edges, and spot vertices that can't be reached. Covers objective 5, and ends with the lecture-ready check.

sections.title: Why BFS finds the fewest edges
text: Imagine the vertices as balls and the edges as strings of equal length. Lift the graph up by ball A and let it hang. Every ball hangs at a height equal to its fewest-edges distance from A.
BFS reads the graph the same way, one level down at a time. So the *first* time BFS finds a vertex, it has found it by a route with the fewest edges, because every shorter level was finished first.

chapters.label: Balls and strings
chapters.caption: Think of the vertices as balls and the edges as strings of equal length.

chapters.label: Lift by A
chapters.caption: Lift the whole graph up by A.

chapters.label: They settle
chapters.caption: Each ball hangs at its fewest-edges distance from A.

chapters.label: Levels
chapters.caption: B and C hang one string down. D and E hang two.

chapters.label: F stays down
chapters.caption: F isn't tied to anything, so it can't be lifted. It's unreachable.

sections.q: BFS first finds E on level 2. Could there be a route from A to E with only 1 edge?
sections.why: A 1-edge route would have put E on level 1, and level 1 is finished before level 2 starts.

sections.title: Remember where each vertex came from
text: To get the route, not just its length, BFS writes down a **parent** for every vertex it finds: the vertex that was being served when it was found.

sections.q: Why is D's parent B, not C?
sections.a: B is served before C, so B finds D first.
sections.why: When C is served, D is already found and nothing changes.

sections.title: Retrace the route backwards
text: Start at the goal and follow parents back to the start, then reverse. For E: E → C → A, reversed: **A, C, E** (2 edges).

chapters.label: Parents
chapters.caption: BFS remembers a parent for every vertex it finds.

chapters.label: Start at E
chapters.caption: To find the route to E, start at E.

chapters.label: Follow parents back
chapters.caption: Follow the parents back: E, C, A.

chapters.label: Turn it around
chapters.caption: Turn it around: A, C, E. That's 2 edges.

chapters.label: Two shortest routes
chapters.caption: D has two shortest routes. BFS gives the one it found first.

source: if n not in parent:          # the parent map is also the found set
return None                      # never found: can't be reached

tasks.q: Predict, then run: the route from A to D.
tasks.why: B is served before C, so D's parent is B. A, C, D is just as short.

tasks.q: Predict, then run: the route from E to B.
tasks.why: From E: C, then A and D, then B is found from A first.

tasks.q: Predict, then run: the route from A to F.
tasks.why: F never gets a parent, so it can't be reached.

questions.q: Type the shortest route from A to D.
hints: Follow D's parent back to A.

sections.title: There can be more than one shortest route
text: A–B–D and A–C–D both have 2 edges. BFS gives A, B, D only because B comes before C in A's list.
Both answers are right, and the route checker accepts any route with the fewest edges.

sections.title: Vertices you can't reach
text: F has no edges, so it never joins the queue, never gets a parent, and `shortest_path` returns `None`.
A vertex BFS never finds can't be reached from the start, however long you search.

sections.q: From which vertices can you reach F?

sections.title: Count edges, not vertices, and not km
text: The route A, C, E has 3 vertices but **2 edges**. Its length is 2.
BFS's "shortest" means fewest edges. If edges had distances in km (a weighted graph), the fewest edges might not be the shortest drive. That needs Dijkstra's algorithm, covered later in COS212.

sections.title: Practice exercises
text: Longer questions. Try each one on paper first.

items.q: Run BFS from E and write the parent map. Then give the route from E to B.
items.a: C←E, A←C, D←C, B←A. Route E, C, A, B (3 edges).

items.q: What is the shortest route from B to E, and its length?
items.a: B, A, C, E: 3 edges. B, D, C, E is equally short.

items.q: A friend says the route A, C, E has length 3. What went wrong?
items.a: They counted vertices. Length is the number of edges: 2.

items.q: Add the edge B–E. What does BFS give for A to E now?
items.a: A, B, E. Still 2 edges, but now found through B because B is served first.

sections.title: Lecture-ready check
text: One question per objective (two for objective 5). After the last one you get your readiness report: each objective is marked **Ready** or **Review**, with a link back to the section and a Retry button.

questions.no: F's list is empty. E has one edge, to C.
C is joined to A, D and E.
questions.ok: Yes. C's neighbours are A, D and E.

questions.q: What is the BFS order from C?
questions.no: C adds A, D and E (level 1). Then A adds B (level 2).
questions.ok: Yes. Level 1 is A, D, E; then B.

questions.q: Explain in a sentence: why is D marked as found when B adds it to the queue?
questions.model: So C can't add D a second time: D is already in the found set when C is served.
questions.no: Have another look at section 03 of Module 3: the bug where D joins twice.

questions.q: What is the fewest number of edges from B to E?
questions.no: B → A → C → E (or B → D → C → E): 3 edges.
questions.ok: Yes. B, A, C, E is 3 edges.

questions.q: Which vertices can't be reached from D?
questions.no: Only F: it has no edges.

topics.recap: BFS finds the fewest-edges route by remembering parents. A vertex it never finds can't be reached.
